tokens: "You are a friendly, patient study companion for someone learning Python "
"and AI agents. You remember the learner between conversations through "
"long-term memory, because a conversation alone is forgotten. When they "
"share something lasting (their name, goals, what they find hard, what "
"they finished, how they like to learn), save it with remember_fact, one "
"fact per call. Use what you remember to personalise explanations and "

cards.title: It forgets mid-chat
cards.body: A reply or message isn't appended to the history you send.

cards.body: You trimmed between a pair. Cut only where a turn starts.

cards.body: Two writers at once in SQLite. Keep transactions short, or use PostgreSQL.

items.q: Design memory for a tutoring agent used by thousands of students.
items.a: Per-student rows in **PostgreSQL**; a **window + running summary** per session; **long-term facts** saved via tools and injected by relevance; secrets refused in code; **retention** and **delete-my-data**; isolation tests; embeddings for recall at scale.
items.trap: One giant shared history, or letting the model choose the user id.

items.q: A user asks you to delete their data. What must happen?
items.a: Delete their **facts, sessions and messages** (and backups and logs, per policy), confirm it, and make sure nothing reloads it. In code: one transaction filtered by user, cascades for children, and a test.
items.trap: Deleting only the facts and forgetting stored conversations.

items.text: The API is stateless: memory is data your code sends
Short-term: a window of recent turns, cut at turn starts
Summary: old turns folded into a running summary
Long-term: facts via tools, relevant ones in the system prompt
SQLite: parameters, transactions, user_id, retention, deletion

scenes.question: Why does a chatbot "remember" earlier messages in a conversation?
options: The model learns during the chat
Your code resends the history with each request
The API key keeps a session
scenes.explain: The Messages API is stateless. Memory within a chat is the history your code sends every time.

scenes.question: Where must a sliding window cut the conversation?
options: Exactly N messages from the end
Where a turn starts: a user message with plain text
scenes.explain: Cutting at a turn start keeps each tool_use with its tool_result. Tool results are user messages, but don't start a turn.

scenes.question: What is the main trade-off of summary memory?
options: Details can be lost, and it costs an extra call
It can't be saved to disk
scenes.explain: A summary keeps the gist small, but exact details may be dropped, and summarizing is one more model call.

scenes.question: The model calls remember_fact with a user's password. What should happen?
options: Your code refuses it and returns a tool error
scenes.explain: Prompts guide; code enforces. The memory layer refuses secrets and the model receives an error observation.

scenes.question: Which query is safe from SQL injection?
scenes.code:
a) conn.execute(f"SELECT * FROM facts WHERE user_id = '{u}'")
b) conn.execute("SELECT * FROM facts WHERE user_id = ?", (u,))
c) conn.execute("SELECT * FROM facts WHERE user_id = '" + u + "'")
d) conn.execute("SELECT * FROM facts WHERE user_id = '%s'" % u)
scenes.explain: Only b passes the value as a parameter. The others paste the value into the SQL text, so input can change the query.

captions.text: Welcome back.
The storage, the memory and the command line are ready.
Now we read the agent's turn line by line, run a demo across two days, use every
privacy feature on purpose, and look at the tests.
Then we wrap up the module with interview questions, a quiz, and your extension
challenge.
First, the system prompt.
As in Module 3, it explains why: the companion remembers through long-term memory,
because a conversation alone is forgotten.
It says what's worth saving, one fact per call, and to use what it remembers to
personalise explanations and quizzes.
And never to save secrets.
Remember, the prompt asks, but the code enforces.
Here's one turn.
We remember how many messages there were, then run the turn.
If the turn didn't end with an answer, a refusal, a cut off reply, too many steps,
we remove its messages.
Never save half a turn.
After a good answer, compact folds old turns into the summary, if we're over the
limit.
That's lesson three.
An API error undoes the turn too, and is reported.
And finally, the whole session is saved in one transaction, as in lesson five.
Inside the turn: add the user's message, and build the system prompt for this
message, with the relevant facts and the summary.
Then the loop from Module 4.
Each reply is stored as plain JSON blocks, so it can be saved to the database, and
sent again tomorrow.
No tool calls means the model has answered.
Otherwise, every memory tool call runs, a refused secret becomes an error result,
and all the results go back in one message, as in Module 5.
Now the demo.
It's the next day: a new session called tue.
The conversation from mon isn't sent at all.
What's my name?
A new, empty session.
But the answer is Anuj, from long-term memory in the system prompt.
Quiz me.
It remembered that I find recursion hard, so the question is about recursion.
That's what memory is for: personal help.
Now, forget that I find recursion hard.
Two steps: recall finds the fact and its number, then forget fact deletes it.
And a password.
The model tried to save it, and our code refused.
The error went back to the model as an observation.
Another user, Riya, asks the same question.
She doesn't get my name.
Every query filters by user.
Now we lower the summary limit, to see compaction.
The footer says: two old messages summarized.

On top, the running summary.
Then the recent turns, word for word.
We show the first and last lines here.

summary.
Retention.
Pretend it's January: purge deletes sessions not used for thirty days.
Both are gone, with their messages.
And delete me asks first, then deletes every fact and session of mine, and nobody
else's.
The tests run the real agent, tools and SQLite against the fake model, with a new
temporary database for every test.

Forty-one tests: memory, the database, the conversation, the tools, the agent and
